correctness.rationale: Independent row choices give iid signs and exact binomial rho. Direct 2x2 Gram computation proves the coefficient formula; the denominator is nonzero almost surely even in collision cases. Gaussian polar coordinates give conditional CDF and bounded support for |rho|<1. At |rho|=1 independent Gaussian sum and difference give an exact standard Cauchy ratio, with event mass 2^(1-m). Remaining finite binomial components are bounded. The far-tail and iff p<1 moment statements follow exactly for all finite m. The packaged script performs arithmetic and quadrature checks on these identities only, not an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The exact coefficient identity and the Cauchy ratio observation were already published in Song--Zhang 2026; they are not claimed new. Its inspected Section 3 proves a nonvanishing high-probability obstruction, whereas the final claim is the exact finite-m binomial mixture, the collision-only Cauchy mass 2^(1-m), the sharp tail beyond a finite support cutoff, and the iff p<1 moment law. Full accessible primary texts of both earlier sign-diagonal SRHT papers concern different sketch distributions; published-finding corpus semantic queries and recoverable own ledger claims showed no implication covering this exact law. The comparison remains best-knowledge and is not an independent priority certificate.

value.rationale: The source identifies the Gaussian-diagonal sketch as a natural but failing attempt to obtain robust coordinate-wise regression. Quantifying its exact finite-sample risk is a motivated missing guarantee: every finite sketch size has infinite expected absolute and squared coefficient error due to exponentially rare row-sign collisions, even when the original design is full-rank unit norm and the estimator is a.s. unique. The exact tail threshold and collision probability distinguish high-probability from integrated error criteria and guide whether row-sampling or resampling modifications can remove this obstruction. It is not a routine restatement of the source's constant-probability lower bound.
